sections.history: Tiruvetkalam lies in the Chola country on the northern side of the Kaveri, a short distance from Chidambaram, and is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the shrines hymned by the Tevaram saints. Sambandar and Appar are recorded as having sung here, which places the worship of the site firmly in the seventh century. The name is usually read as the hunting ground of the Lord, a reference to the story that has made the place famous. The structural temple is traditionally credited to the Cholas, though some accounts speak of an earlier brick shrine, and in 1914 it was rebuilt in stone through the generosity of a Chettiar patron from Kanadukathan. In the twentieth century the growing campus of Annamalai University closed around the temple, so that this old sanctuary now sits among lecture halls and lawns, still kept in daily worship.
sections.architecture: The temple covers about two acres within concentric rectangular walls. A three-tiered rajagopuram opens the eastern side, and beyond it the way leads through a pillared hall and an ardha mandapa to the sanctum of Pasupatheeswarar. The goddess Nalla Nayaki is honoured in a shrine in the front hall that faces south. The pillars of the goddess's shrine are carved with scenes from the Arjuna legend, among them Shiva in the guise of a hunter, and a figure of Parvati with her hair unbound is counted among the temple's notable images. Bamboo is the sacred tree of the shrine, a reminder of the forest in which Arjuna is said to have kept his vigil.
sections.legends: The legend of Tiruvetkalam belongs to the Mahabharata. During the Pandavas' exile Arjuna withdrew to a forest of bamboo to perform austerities for the Pasupata, the weapon of Shiva that he would need in the war to come. While he was absorbed in prayer, a wild boar rushed upon him, and both Arjuna and a hunter loosed an arrow at the same moment. The two argued over who had struck the beast, and the quarrel grew into a trial of strength in which Arjuna was overcome. Humbled, he turned to Shiva in worship, and the hunter revealed himself as the Lord, who had come with Parvati to test his steadfastness. Pleased, Shiva granted him the Pasupata, and from this the Lord of the place is called Pasupatheeswarar. Tradition adds that the linga bears a mark from Arjuna's blow, a sign that even the strike of a proud warrior is received with grace.
sections.festivals: The most prominent festival is the Tamil New Year in the month of Chithirai (April), when the deities are honoured with special worship and procession. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed here as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tiruvetkalam is a quiet visit, and an easy one to pair with Chidambaram. The temple lies in the rear part of the Annamalai University grounds, so you arrive through the campus and then step into a calm old courtyard. Pause beneath the eastern gopuram, come to the sanctum of Pasupatheeswarar, and then spend a little time at the goddess's shrine, where the carved pillars tell the story of Arjuna and the hunter in stone. Devotees come here seeking strength and protection in a time of struggle, and many remember the saints' hymns while circling the shrine. On most days the courtyard is peaceful and unhurried.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands inside the Annamalai University campus at Annamalai Nagar, a few kilometres from Chidambaram. Enter by the university's main gate and follow the road toward the rear of the campus, near the music college. Chidambaram has the nearest railway station and bus stand, and auto-rickshaws and local buses run to Annamalai Nagar. Puducherry and Chennai are the nearest airports, both several hours away by road.
